clinicalPearls: A pinguecula is a yellowish-white, slightly raised amorphous deposit on the bulbar conjunctiva, characteristically at the nasal (and later temporal) limbus within the interpalpebral fissure but, unlike a pterygium, it does NOT encroach onto the cornea.

It represents actinic (ultraviolet) elastotic degeneration of the subepithelial conjunctival stroma; chronic sun, wind and dust exposure are the principal drivers, so it is commoner in outdoor workers and low-latitude populations.
The great majority are asymptomatic and require only reassurance; lubricants suffice for mild irritation or foreign-body sensation.

Pingueculitis denotes episodic inflammation with localised hyperaemia and swelling, often after intense ultraviolet exposure or ocular-surface dryness, and is managed with lubricants and a short course of a mild topical anti-inflammatory.
Photoprotection with wrap-around sunglasses and a broad-brimmed hat is the key preventive and progression-limiting measure.
Excision is reserved for cosmetic concern, recurrent pingueculitis, interference with contact-lens wear, or diagnostic uncertainty; surgery carries a risk of scarring and recurrence.

A lesion that grows atypically, becomes nodular, develops feeder vessels, pigmentation or leukoplakia, or does not respect the limbus should raise suspicion of ocular surface squamous neoplasia rather than a benign pinguecula.
Pinguecula and pterygium share the same actinic aetiology and frequently coexist; a pinguecula may be a precursor stage but the two are distinguished by corneal involvement.
reference.pathophysiology: Chronic ultraviolet and environmental (wind, dust, dryness) exposure induces actinic damage to the bulbar conjunctival stroma within the interpalpebral zone, where light is focused nasally by the anterior segment. The result is elastotic degeneration: fragmentation and abnormal accumulation of elastin-like fibrillar material in the substantia propria, with hyalinisation of collagen, secondary calcification in some lesions, and a thinned or occasionally thickened overlying epithelium. Because the process is confined to the subepithelial conjunctiva and does not cross the limbal barrier, the cornea is spared, distinguishing it from pterygium.
additionalDifferentials: Pterygium (fibrovascular growth crossing the limbus onto cornea)
Conjunctival intraepithelial neoplasia / ocular surface squamous neoplasia
Bitot spot of vitamin A deficiency
Limbal nodule of phlyctenular or nodular scleritis
additionalInvestigations: Slit-lamp biomicroscopy to characterise the lesion and confirm the cornea is spared
Documentation with anterior-segment photography for serial comparison
Assessment of tear film and ocular surface (tear break-up time, staining) for associated dryness
Anterior-segment optical coherence tomography where depth or atypia needs clarification
Excisional or incisional biopsy with histopathology if neoplasia is suspected
Corneal topography if a coexisting pterygium is inducing astigmatism
redFlags: Progressive growth, nodularity, feeder vessels, pigmentation or leukoplakia suggesting ocular surface squamous neoplasia or melanoma
Encroachment onto the cornea indicating pterygium rather than pinguecula
Persistent or recurrent inflammation unresponsive to lubricants and photoprotection
Rapid change in size, colour or vascularity of a previously stable lesion
reference.prognosis: An entirely benign degenerative lesion with an excellent prognosis; most remain stable and asymptomatic for life. Even after excision for cosmesis or recurrent pingueculitis the outlook is good, though scarring and recurrence are recognised.
pitfalls: Mistaking an atypical conjunctival neoplasm for a benign pinguecula and delaying biopsy
Confusing a pinguecula with an early pterygium; the defining feature is whether the lesion crosses the limbus onto the cornea
Over-treating an asymptomatic lesion with prolonged topical steroids, risking raised intraocular pressure and cataract
Attributing all interpalpebral irritation to the pinguecula while overlooking coexisting dry eye disease
Assuming excision is curative without warning the patient about recurrence and conjunctival scarring
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology, Basic and Clinical Science Course — External Disease and Cornea
management: Reassure and observe, as most lesions are asymptomatic benign actinic degeneration requiring no active treatment
Advise photoprotection with wrap-around sunglasses and a broad-brimmed hat as the key measure to limit progression
Relieve mild irritation and foreign-body sensation with ocular lubricants and management of any coexisting dry eye
Treat episodes of pingueculitis with lubricants and a short course of a mild topical anti-inflammatory such as a weak corticosteroid or topical NSAID
Reserve surgical excision for cosmetic concern, recurrent pingueculitis, contact-lens intolerance or diagnostic uncertainty, counselling on scarring and recurrence risk
Document with anterior-segment photography for serial comparison and biopsy any lesion where neoplasia is suspected
